item.title: Mourning the Silence of Civic Education
item.description:
This letter, by Chan-Yul Kim, 16, of McNeil High School in Austin, Texas, is one of the winners of The Learning Network’s Student Open Letter Contest, for which we received 11,185 entries. You can find the work of all the winners, as we publish them, here.

Dear Texas House Committee on Public Education,

This February, hundreds of my classmates, armed with megaphones and spray-painted card stock, flooded out of school and marched to our local Whataburger in protest of ICE. Sifting through overwhelming texts, I noticed this horde was far from an organized unit, ranging from furious denouncers of ICE to kids who just wanted a burger.

I wonder what stood out to you, the committee spearheading Texas education, when our protest went viral. Were you proud or disapproving of what the crowd chanted? Uncomfortable with the stir in Texas schools?

Because while the flashy headlines may have made it onto your desks, the wake-up call that got my attention was the disturbing, out-of-place silence the next day.

Hearing from an outspoken activist about an encounter with law enforcement, the athlete who just wanted to skip her class, or the immigrant fearing repercussions of activism could have amplified unheard voices and allowed us to discover varying perspectives.

Instead, all I saw in class the day after the walkout was an awkward avoidance of the … “situation.” Our classrooms were mute, with teachers scared of walking the tightrope of politics and students torn between political curiosity and fear of offending a friend.

When your policies deem a protest on my own campus as too “controversial” for the classroom, they abandon students to achieve political literacy alone and invite extremism by ceding cross-partisan understanding.

Although intended to prevent partisanship out of fear that teachers will dictate what kids believe, your policies have induced another dilemma: they obliterated engagement with subjects that matter today. Because educators are now exposed to accusations of bias, schools neglect their responsibility in teaching us how to form our own educated beliefs.

When schools forfeit civic education, my average disinterested classmate will turn to social media for their “education.” The New York Times reports that the largest social media platforms function as echo chambers that radicalize user biases while drowning out the moderate majority. In a time when politics is characterized by bitterness and panic, we can’t afford to put our youth in the hands of an extremist algorithm.

Thankfully, civic education doesn’t have to cost us classroom neutrality; in fact, The Guardian reports that out of more than three dozen civics projects suspended following 2021 Texas legislation, “the vast majority dealt with hyperlocal, nonpartisan issues.” Teachers can cultivate critical thinking through political engagement without brainwashing students into their partisan agendas!

Please — it’s not too late to make room for difficult conversations. Prepare us to become critical thinkers who can handle civic responsibilities. Classrooms are unique spaces where teachers can moderate safe discussions, so develop frameworks for educators to empower nonpartisan communication rather than blanket-banning all sensitive topics.

If you get this right, you can create an opportunity for us to cherish diversity and become sensible citizens. Otherwise, we’ll have to stake our future on a generation that can only solve problems by walking to Whataburger.

Sincerely,Someone who may never hear the other side

Works Cited

Hsu, Tiffany, et al. “Elections and Disinformation Are Colliding Like Never Before in 2024.” The New York Times, 9 Jan. 2024.

Lehrer-Small, Asher. “Texas Guts ‘Woke Civics.’ Now Kids Can’t Engage in a Key Democratic Process.” The Guardian, 1 May 2023.

item.title: ‘The Boy in the Striped Pajamas’: The Cost of Fictionalizing the Holocaust
item.description:
This letter, by Orly Kochinski, 16, of Northwood High School in Irvine, Calif., is one of the winners of The Learning Network’s Student Open Letter Contest, for which we received 11,185 entries. You can find the work of all the winners, as we publish them, here.

Dear Members of the Irvine Unified School District Board of Education,

I am the great-granddaughter of five Holocaust survivors: Chaya Kochinski, Natan Kochinski, Shoshana Amitai, Tuli Schiff and Evi Schiff. To merely call them “survivors” feels inadequate. They lived through the unimaginable: starved, beaten and dehumanized.

So, when my eighth-grade class was assigned to read “The Boy in the Striped Pajamas,” I was stunned. Instead of centering the Jewish victims, the novel asks students to sympathize with Bruno, the son of a high-ranking Nazi commandant. It presents a historically impossible scenario where a German child wanders right up to the electrified, high-voltage fences of Auschwitz to befriend a Jewish boy. The book continues to paint a “fantasy Auschwitz” where barriers are easily bypassed, prisoners receive medical accommodations, and Bruno remains plausibly ignorant of the horrors around him.

Upon researching further, I found I was not alone in my reaction. In fact, the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum explicitly states that the book “should be avoided by anyone who studies or teaches the history of the Holocaust.” By portraying Jewish victims as passive, the novel simplifies a horrific reality to make it more palatable. We cannot hide from the past, and we cannot rewrite it. To ensure history is never repeated, we must teach the brutal truth.

While some educators argue that students must be taught to examine narration and evaluate historical accuracy, how can students decipher truth from fiction when they do not yet know what the truth is? Because this is often their first exposure to the Holocaust, they are not equipped to recognize the damaging inaccuracies in the book. It is no coincidence that shortly after reading this novel, a classmate confronted me with the claim that Jews could have prevented the Holocaust if only they had “tried hard enough.” Claims like these stem from the book’s ignorant portrayal of Jewish victims as passive characters waiting to be helped, rather than people trapped in a state-sponsored system of annihilation. My great-grandparents did not endure lasting trauma simply to have their suffering reduced to the suggestion that they could have prevented it if only they had “tried hard enough.”

My letter is not purely a critique; it is a call for action. In The New York Times article “Holocaust Is Fading From Memory, Survey Finds” Maggie Astor notes that 41 percent of U.S. millennials believe two million or fewer Jews were killed during the Holocaust, a vast understatement of the actual six million. Furthermore, 66 percent do not know what Auschwitz was. By removing this fiction from schools and replacing it with the visceral testimony of Elie Wiesel’s “Night” or the graphic truth of Leon Leyson’s “The Boy on the Wooden Box,” we can begin to rectify Holocaust education.

I urge the school board: honor the millions who were murdered, and the few, like my great-grandparents, who survived, by finally trusting students with the truth. Only by teaching this history correctly can we truly honor the promise of “Never again.”

Thank you,Orly

Works Cited

Astor, Maggie. “Holocaust Is Fading From Memory, Survey Finds.” The New York Times, 12 April 2018.

Flood, Alison. “The Boy In The Striped Pyjamas Author Defends Work From Criticism by Auschwitz Memorial.” The Guardian, 7 Jan. 2020.
